name: Nora Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; this is confidential, and your name won't go in our findings. Could you describe a normal day on the crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, 43, a junior lineworker. I check the insulating blankets and the lower controls on the bucket truck, then I ride out with the crew and help set up around the pole. I'm still learning, so I repeat the lead's checks before I handle anything near the line.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what is the hardest part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the crew can solve a problem together and leave the street safer than we found it. I get home tired from watching every movement, and my partner and I have a mortgage and two children, ages 11 and 15.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I can use the AI stock tool to count insulators, but the crew still checks each one for damage. A small saving on inventory doesn't change the physical checks we do at the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect this small version to take my job because I'm mostly doing hands-on work. My pay is modest and our savings are thin, so the mortgage still puts pressure on every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep practising blanket placement and bucket controls with the lead. I would try the AI stock tool only after the experienced crew checked its counts against the parts shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm steady about the work but anxious about the household budget. A few minutes saved at the depot does not give us a larger cushion for a surprise bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want checked before the crew trusts a stock count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want someone to compare the count with the labelled bins and look at the insulating blankets for wear. The tool cannot tell whether a blanket is cracked or damp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and your partner do when a household bill is higher than expected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We look at what can wait and leave the mortgage payment alone. If the refrigerator still works, we don't replace it just because a newer model is on sale.

I don't treat a faster inventory as a replacement for **pole checks**.
think: I don't expect this mild change to remove my **hands-on job**.
I still worry about the **mortgage** because our savings are thin.
do: Keep practising **blanket placement** and bucket controls with the crew lead.
Use the **AI stock tool** after experienced workers check its part counts.
feel: I'm steady about work but **anxious** about a surprise household bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people on the pole see things the schedule can't see from a desk. A better plan might get the right truck there, but the lead still has to decide how we set the barriers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose some hours if dispatch rearranges work and the junior crew is assigned fewer jobs. I don't know another local employer that could quickly replace that pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lead to show me the new AI dispatch screen after it has been used on real callouts. I would keep taking field shifts and sign up for employer-paid bucket-truck emergency-control practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about my hours but open to a tool after the crew proves it works. I want the company to explain whether changed scheduling alters the number of junior shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before accepting the new dispatch screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare its arrival times with the actual callout sheet and ask the lead to explain any difference. If it keeps sending the truck to a closed access road, I'd stick with the verified route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about the paid bucket-truck training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a date, paid hours, and a lead who can watch the emergency lowering drill. I don't want a web lesson to count as practice on a machine.

I want the lead to decide how the crew sets **barriers**.
think: I worry that dispatch changes could reduce **junior shifts**.
I know of few local employers that could replace **lost pay**.
do: Learn the **AI dispatch screen** after the lead tests it on callouts.
Keep taking field shifts and sign up for paid **bucket-truck practice**.
feel: I'm **anxious** about hours, though I can accept a proven tool.
S1.quote: I'd say the people on the pole see things the schedule can't see from a desk.
fieldNote: She asks to compare screen estimates with the **actual callout sheet**.

steps.text: Keep taking field shifts while dispatch work changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company to say how many field crews it expects to keep and when it will give notice. The planning and records work changes first, but a robot date around 2031 means our field jobs are also exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may have a few years before robots reach the bucket work, but the employer can reduce crews sooner. My mortgage and thin savings make it hard to wait for a different job if my hours stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the worker representative for a written notice rule and paid practical training. In 2028 I would not move into records or planning as a safe career, because AGI can do that thinking work. In 2029, if I still have shifts, I'd take a company-paid insulating-blanket course and keep working on field repairs while they're available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious that the company could cut my shift before the robots arrive. A paid course would help me learn, but I can't pay tuition or lose wages for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What household expense would you change first if the roster dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause our planned replacement of the refrigerator and keep the current one running if a repair is safe. I wouldn't cut the children's school supplies or miss the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the blanket course to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want an instructor to show how to position each blanket and inspect it afterward. It should be paid working time, because my household can't carry the cost of an unpaid course.

say: I want the company to state its **field crew numbers** and notice dates.
I know the **2031 robot date** reaches hands-on work too.
think: I may have field work for a few years, but the company could cut **crews sooner**.
I won't treat **records or planning** as safe work after AGI.
do: Ask the worker representative for **notice and paid practice**.
Take the company-paid **insulating-blanket course** in 2029 if shifts remain.
Keep the current **refrigerator** running if a repair is safe and protect school supplies.
feel: I'm **anxious** about losing wages before robots arrive.
S2.quote: I would ask the company to say how many field crews it expects to keep and when it will give notice.
fieldNote: She seeks a paid, **hands-on blanket course** rather than tuition-funded study.
She protects the mortgage and children's supplies before replacing a **working refrigerator**.
She understands **physical work** will be exposed after the thinking-work shift.

steps.text: Ask the worker representative to secure notice before crew reductions
Take the paid insulating-blanket course in 2029 if employed
Keep using the refrigerator if it can be repaired safely

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the utility time to train us while there are still regular jobs to practise on. It should publish what practical qualifications it will pay for before the 2034 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when AGI arrives and 51 when robots arrive. I could improve my skills before then, but I don't know if this utility will keep the same number of field crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the lead for supervised practice with the insulated bucket and keep a record of each task. In 2032, the first year after AGI, I'd take an employer-paid bucket rescue course, continue working field shifts, and compare an actual posted vacancy before considering a transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because five years is time to train but not enough to assume I can find another employer. I need any course to fit around paid shifts and the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you consider that posted vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the wage, shift schedule, and training requirement with my current job. If the opening is only a short contract or pays less, I would stay where I am while the field work continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the bucket rescue course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a qualified lead to supervise the emergency-lowering practice and sign my record. I need to know the certificate covers a task I can actually perform, not promise that a job will last.

say: I say five years gives the utility time to **train field crews**.
I want the company to publish **paid qualifications** before 2034.
think: I'll be **48** at AGI and **51** when robots arrive.
I may improve, but I don't know how many **field crews** will remain.
do: Ask for supervised **bucket practice** and record each task now.
Take an employer-paid rescue course and keep field shifts in **2032**.
Compare an actual **posted vacancy** before considering a transfer.
feel: I'm **anxious**, because a course does not guarantee another employer.
S3.quote: I'd say five years gives the utility time to train us while there are still regular jobs to practise on.
fieldNote: She wants a **signed practical record** and a real emergency-lowering drill.
She will compare a vacancy's **pay and contract length** before transferring.
She needs **paid hours** because savings cannot cover unpaid course time.

steps.text: Keep working field shifts while regular jobs remain
Take the employer-paid bucket rescue course in 2032
Wait for a posted vacancy and compare its actual terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the long notice gives the utility time to tell crews what it knows about staffing and paid training. I wouldn't say my current linework is safe after robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when robots do. A decade gives me more time to qualify for other field tasks, but office planning and records won't protect me once AGI can do thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask for the next paid practical course and keep my sign-off record current. In 2037, if I still have shifts, I'd compare the actual roster and wages, take employer-paid bucket training if offered, and talk with my partner and adult children before deciding whether to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me options, but our savings still cover less than a month today. I'm anxious about current bills and the possibility that a later robot rollout reaches the work I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would have to be true before your household moved for a different job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2037 our children will be 22 and 26. My partner and I would talk with them about their work and home commitments before moving for my job, since I can't assume grown children will follow us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you decide whether to keep linework?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see the actual field duties, paid training dates, and what hours the utility expects to offer in 2037. I could compare that with the mortgage and talk with our children, but I know no roster can promise work through 2039.

say: I want the utility's **staffing and training plan** before the last year.
think: I'll be **53** at AGI and **56** when robots arrive.
I won't rely on **planning or records** to protect my income.
do: Request the next **paid practical course** and keep sign-offs current.
Compare the **actual roster** and wages before choosing whether to stay.
Wait for the roster and **talk with our children** before deciding whether to move.
feel: I'm **anxious** about today's bills and later robot exposure.
S4.quote: I'd say the long notice gives the utility time to tell crews what it knows about staffing and paid training.
fieldNote: She treats **adult children's commitments** as part of a relocation decision.
She knows no current field qualification guarantees work past the **robot date**.
She wants an actual **review date** before making household plans.

steps.text: Keep the sign-off record current while continuing field work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots may arrive around 2031 before I build a stronger qualification record. Paid training, a clear roster, and time to practise would help more than a general promise that workers can adapt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: An apprenticeship with paid practice gives a worker something real to carry into the next decision. I want the company to say which course it will pay for and how many hours I can practise.

headlineQuote: An apprenticeship with paid practice gives a worker something real to carry into the next decision.
portrait: Nora is a **43-year-old junior** lineworker with a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She adopts proven work tools carefully and prioritizes **hands-on training**.
Her **thin savings** mean reduced shifts would quickly affect household bills.
She seeks paid qualifications and confirmed rosters, while accepting no trade is **guaranteed safe**.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries her most because robots may arrive around 2031 before she builds a stronger reserve.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **practical training**, a clear roster and time to practise would help her plan.
